text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's Albanian newspapers. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Nick Pavaci, the leader of the Former Political Prisoners Association in the northern town of Shkoder and one of the leaders of the United Right (UR), has been beaten up. UR accused ruling Democratic Party extremists of orchestrating the attack.
- Tirana's new mayor, Albert Brojka of the ruling Democratic Party, has ordered illegal kiosks to be removed from the city centre.
- Valer Xheka, the leader of the Independent Trade Unions, and ruling Democratic Party MP Azem Hajdari who proclaimed himself the union's new head have both taken their struggle to the regions.
- The European Union's PHARE programme, which provides technical aid to East European countries, has given Albania 33 million ECUs for three years, with road infrastructure to get the lion's share.
- Declan Ganley, the head of the Anglo-Adriatic investment fund, says they are ready to invest more than 30,000 privatisation vouchers in strategic industries up for sale.
- The Albanian government and the International Monetary Fund are locked in a tacit battle over suspected pyramid money schemes.

- Several opposition parties have agreed Albania should hold a referendum on whether the country should be a monarchy or a republic before a Constitutional Assembly convenes to draw up a constitution.

- Mining minister Abdyl Xhaja, told miners that negotiations were continuing with Germany's Preussag AG on a possible deal to sell 80 percent of Albania's chrome industry. He said the mines could only be saved by large-scale foreign capital.

- Albanian Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu said certain political groups had manipulated the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, which pulled its monitors out of Albania's controversial parliamentary elections.

- Rrapush Xhaferri, who launched a high-interest money scheme, denies his operation involves either pyramid schemes or money laundering. He says investors' quotas make up 2.7 percent of his capital, whilst the rest is his own inherited wealth.
